Tukārām is one of the greatest mystic saint-poets of Maharashtra whose अभङ्गस् (devotional songs in Marāṭhī) (See ABHAṄGAS.), which run into thousands, are popular even now.
TukārāmHe was born at Dehu, a village 22½kms. (14 miles) away from the city of Pune. He belonged to the Marāṭha caste considered by many as belonging to the śūdra group.
He was married at an early age but lost his wife and a son as also his parents when a terrible famine ravaged the village. He was married again, Āvaḷi (or Jījābāi) being the name of his second wife.
Basically he was inclined towards a spiritual life through the path of भक्ति or devotion. Repeated failures in life intensified this bent of मिन्द्. Hence he started studying religious works and spend the time singing devotional songs. He received a मन्त्र (holy name) in dream from one Bābājī चैतन्य which मन्त्र he started repeating as much as possible. In another dream experience, नाम्देव् (A.

-1320), another great saint of Maharashtra, entrusted him with the task of composing अभङ्गस्, to complete his own unfinished task.
From now onwards, new अभङ्गस् containing gems of spiritual truths, started flowing from his mouth. Larger and larger number of common people started taking part in his congregations of devotional मुसिच् and discourses.
This roused the jealousy and anger of the orthodox ब्राह्मणस् who tried their best to harm him but were soon chastened and converted to become his ardent followers.
However, these detractors once succeeded in forcing तुकाराम् to drown the manuscripts of his अभङ्गस् in the Indrāyaṇī river. But Lord पाण्डुरङ्ग Viṭṭhala (a form of कृष्ण, popular in Maharashtra) restored them to their true owner.
On another occasion, तुकाराम् miraculously saved the king Śivājī (A.

-1680) from being captured by the Moghuls.
On the last day of his life, तुकाराम् is said to have bodily ascended to हेअवेन् in a divine chariot.
The teachings he has delivered, primarily through his अभङ्गस्, stress the importance of devotion to पाण्डुरङ्ग Viṭṭhala, the power of the divine name, the irrelevance of caste in spiritual life and the futility of religious rituals.
See also ABHAṄGAS and NĀMDEV.
